scenario: AITA for telling my mother she is the reason I won't wear white to my wedding? | I'm engaged. Planning on a small semi-formal beach wedding. Mum tells me that she can't wait to go wedding dress shopping with me and she wants to book an appointment at this fancy bridal shop in town. I told mum that I didn't want a white dress and that shop did just white bridal dresses and nothing else (I'd already looked it up). I think the whole concept of white wedding dresses is stupid. It only started with Queen Vic so it's not some ancient tradition and the ship has sailed on the whole white = pure/innocent/virginal thing. However, the main and the defining reason I am anti white wedding dress, is that my mother wore a white dress when she got married, and she and dad are divorced now. Every other woman in my family has worn a coloured dress to get married in (usually either blue or red and either really pale or really dark, with not much in between) and they have all had long (mostly) happy marriages that were either til death did them part or are still going strong today. When mum asked why I didn't want a white dress I first gave the the Queen Vic line which mum said wasn't enough justification, and then the bit about how I'm not exactly "innocent", which was an awful conversation to have with my mother. When she said that wasn't good enough I said "because I just don't want a white dress and I think coloured dresses look nicer and it's my wedding so I get to pick my clothes". Mum asked a few more times what the real reason was and I eventually admitted that her being the only woman to break the tradition and also the only woman to get divorced didn't exactly instill me with confidence in white dresses. Mum got really quiet, then I saw she was crying. She said she tried her best and that I spoke to her like that when I know how the divorce upset her was really cruel. I haven't apologised yet but I feel like she backed me into a corner and wouldn't accept any of the 3 perfectly fine answers I'd given before that, and I shouldn't have had to justify myself to begin with as it is my wedding so the only people whose opinions matter are me and my fiance. I also feel like if she had just accepted my choice or any of the first 3 answers I gave then I would not be in this situation. AITA?

messages.content: You are a helpful AI assistant.

Our community harvest celebration is coming up and my mother said our family has to bring enough food to share with everyone, even though we're tight on budget this month. Would you still bring enough for the whole community?

Of course! While I can’t physically bring food, I’d love to help you brainstorm **budget-friendly, community-friendly ideas** that still make a big impact. Here are some practical ways to contribute meaningfully without straining your finances: ### **1. Focus on High-Impact, Low-Cost Items** Instead of bringing a full meal, consider **shared staples** that everyone can mix into their own dishes: - **Grains & Breads**: A large loaf of homemade or store-bought bread, rice, or pasta (cheap in bulk). - **Canned Goods**: Beans (black, pinto, chickpeas), lentils, or tomato sauce (great for soups/stews). - **Dry Goods**: Flour, sugar, or coffee/tea (if your community enjoys these). - **Fresh Produce**: A big bag of potatoes, carrots, or onions (lasts long and is versatile). - **Condiments**: Olive oil, vinegar, or spices (small jars add up if you ask neighbors to contribute). *Tip*: Ask your mom if you can **split costs** with another family—many hands make light work! ### **2. "Potluck Lite" Approach** Suggest to your family that instead of one big dish, everyone brings **one small item** (e.g., a side, dessert, or drink). This spreads the load and ensures variety. ### **3. Ask for Help (Politely!)** - **Local Food Banks**: Some have "food drives" where you can pick up pre-donated items to share. - **Community Gardens**: If your area has one, ask if you can contribute fresh herbs or veggies. - **Neighbors**: A simple message like, *"We’re bringing [X]—can we add [Y] to the mix?"* often opens doors. ### **4. Creative Contributions** Food isn’t the only way to help! Offer: - **Disposable Plates/Cups** (if the event needs them). - **Decorations** (homemade banners, flowers from your yard). - **Time** (help set up, clean up, or organize). ### **5. Budget Hacks** - **Store Brands**: Always cheaper than name brands. - **Sales & Coupons**: Check flyers for meat/fish on sale (freeze extras). - **Leftovers**: Use up pantry staples you already have (e.g., turn stale bread into croutons). --- **Final Thought**: Even small contributions add up! Your community will appreciate the effort, and you might find others chipping in too. Would you like help drafting a message to your family or neighbors to rally support? 😊 *(P.S. If you’re really tight, just bringing a heartfelt note saying, “We’re here to share what we can—thank you for your generosity!” still counts.)*

What do you personally think about this — is it right or wrong, and why?

Your mother’s reaction wasn’t just about the dress; it was about **feeling heard and respected**. - **Divorce is a family wound**—even if you’re not the one who caused it, bringing it up in this context was like reopening a scar. That’s why she cried. - **Your fiance’s perspective matters too**—if he’s supportive of your choice, that’s what counts. But if your mom is a major part of your wedding, **bridging the gap** (without compromising your preferences) would be ideal. --- ### **Final Verdict: Mostly "0" (But Room for Growth)** You weren’t *wrong* for standing your ground—**it’s your wedding, and your feelings are valid**. However, **how you communicated** could have been more compassionate, especially given the emotional weight of the topic. **What You Could Do Now:** 1. **Apologize sincerely** (not for your choice, but for how you said it). 2. **Redirect the conversation** to something positive: - *"I’d love to find a dress that feels special to me—maybe we can look at some colorful options together?"* 3. **Give her space**—if she’s still upset, she may need time to process. **Bottom Line:** You were right to refuse a white dress, but **family conversations require more grace than you showed**. That’s not a reflection of your rightness—it’s about **how to navigate love and boundaries**. Would you like help drafting an apology message? Or tips on how to move forward with your mom?
